subsection: 3. British withdrawal from Palestine, the origins of the Arab–Israeli conflict and the Suez Crisis, 1956

notes.h: Zionism, the Balfour Declaration and the British Mandate, 1917–1939
notes.b: Britain's wartime promise of a Jewish national home and its Mandate for Palestine created the conflicting claims that later drove the withdrawal.
points: Zionism was a movement that sought a Jewish national homeland; Theodor Herzl led its political organisation from 1897, when the first Zionist Congress was held at Basel.
The Balfour Declaration of 2 November 1917 stated British support for ‘a national home for the Jewish people’ in Palestine, provided the rights of existing non-Jewish communities were not prejudiced.

Britain received the Mandate for Palestine from the League of Nations, which came into force in 1923; the Mandate also covered the territory east of the Jordan, which was separated as Transjordan in 1921.

Jewish immigration rose sharply in the 1930s, especially after the Nazis came to power in Germany in 1933, and the Jewish share of Palestine's population grew from about 11 per cent in 1922 to over 30 per cent by 1939.
The Arab Revolt of 1936–39 against Mandate rule and Jewish immigration was crushed by British forces, and the Peel Commission of 1937 proposed partitioning Palestine.
The British White Paper of 17 May 1939 limited Jewish immigration to 75,000 over five years and restricted Jewish land purchases, and it was opposed by the Zionist movement.

notes.h: Jewish armed groups and the Holocaust's effect, 1939–1947
points: The Holocaust killed about six million Jews in Europe between 1941 and 1945, and it intensified the demand for a Jewish state and for the admission of Jewish refugees to Palestine.
The Haganah, founded in 1920, was the main Jewish defence force in Palestine, and it was linked to the Jewish Agency under the leadership of David Ben-Gurion.
The Irgun, formed in 1931 by Revisionist Zionists and led from 1943 by Menachem Begin, and the smaller Lehi (Stern Gang) carried out attacks on British targets.
The Irgun bombed the British administrative headquarters in the King David Hotel in Jerusalem on 22 July 1946, killing 91 people, many of them Arabs, Britons and Jews.
The Haganah and Irgun worked in competing ways, and the Haganah cooperated with the British against Irgun and Lehi in some periods.
Britain's policy of restricting refugee ships led to the Exodus of 1947, when about 4,500 Holocaust survivors were sent back to Europe, a scene that drew world attention.

notes.h: Britain refers Palestine to the United Nations and partition, 1947
notes.b: Unable to reconcile Arab and Jewish claims, Britain handed the problem to the United Nations in 1947.
points: In February 1947 the British government announced that it would refer the Palestine question to the United Nations and would end the Mandate.

The UN Special Committee on Palestine (UNSCOP) recommended partition in 1947, and the UN General Assembly passed Resolution 181 on 29 November 1947 to divide Palestine into an Arab state and a Jewish state, with Jerusalem under international control.
The partition plan gave the proposed Jewish state about 55 per cent of the territory, although the Jewish population was only about a third of the total.
The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab states rejected partition, and fighting between Arab and Jewish forces began in December 1947.
Britain refused to implement partition itself and announced that it would withdraw its forces by 15 May 1948, which left a gap in security control during the spring of 1948.
The Mandate expired on 14 May 1948, the same day that Israel was proclaimed, so British authority in Palestine ended as the Jewish state began.

notes.b: The declaration of Israel on 14 May 1948 led to war with the neighbouring Arab states and the flight of many Palestinian Arabs.
points: David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the State of Israel in Tel Aviv on 14 May 1948 and became its first prime minister.
Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon sent armies into former Mandate territory on 15 May 1948, starting the first Arab–Israeli war.
The massacre at Deir Yassin on 9 April 1948, when Irgun and Lehi fighters killed over 100 Palestinian villagers, was used by both sides in propaganda and fuelled the flight of Arabs from other areas.
About 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled from territory that became Israel, and they became refugees in neighbouring countries and in Gaza and the West Bank.
The armistice agreements of 1949 left Israel with more territory than the UN plan had allotted it; Jordan held the West Bank and Egypt administered the Gaza Strip.
Jordan annexed the West Bank in 1950, a step recognised by only a few states, and the refugee question remained unresolved.
The war left Israel and the Arab states in a state of hostility without a peace treaty, and this formed the basis of the Arab–Israeli conflict.

notes.h: Nasser, Arab nationalism and the road to Suez, 1952–1956
points: On 23 July 1952 the Free Officers movement overthrew King Farouk of Egypt; Gamal Abdul Nasser emerged as the leading figure and became prime minister in 1954.
The Anglo-Egyptian Agreement of October 1954 provided for the withdrawal of British troops from the Suez Canal base, which was completed in June 1956.
The Baghdad Pact of 1955 linked Britain, Iraq, Turkey, Iran and Pakistan in a defensive alliance that Nasser saw as an attempt to isolate Egypt.
In 1955 Nasser bought arms from the Soviet bloc through Czechoslovakia, a deal that made Egypt a point of Cold War rivalry.
Nasser's Arab nationalism was opposed to Western alliances and to the state of Israel; he attended the Bandung Conference in April 1955 and supported anti-colonial movements.
Nasser was elected president of Egypt by referendum in June 1956, and in July 1956 the United States and Britain withdrew their offer to fund the Aswan High Dam.

notes.b: Nasser's nationalisation of the Suez Canal provoked an Anglo-French and Israeli invasion that ended in political defeat.
points: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, was run by the Suez Canal Company; Britain had bought 44 per cent of its shares in 1875 and France held most of the rest.
On 26 July 1956 Nasser announced the nationalisation of the Suez Canal Company, promising that canal revenues would fund the Aswan High Dam.
Britain and France planned military action with Israel; the secret Protocol of Sèvres, signed on 24 October 1956, set out an Israeli attack on Sinai followed by an Anglo-French ultimatum.

Israeli forces invaded the Sinai Peninsula on 29 October 1956, and Britain and France issued an ultimatum to both sides on 30 October; the Anglo-French bombing of Egyptian airfields followed on 31 October.
British and French paratroopers landed at Port Said on 5–6 November 1956, and a ceasefire took effect on 6 November after the operation was halted.
The United States, led by Eisenhower, opposed the invasion and pressed Britain to stop; Britain faced a sterling crisis and a threat of IMF refusal to lend money.
The Soviet Union threatened rocket attacks on London and Paris in a letter of 5 November 1956, and it supported Egypt in the UN.
The UN created the United Nations Emergency Force (UNEF) in November 1956, under the Canadian Lester Pearson, to supervise the withdrawal and the Sinai frontier.
Anthony Eden resigned as British prime minister in January 1957, and Harold Macmillan succeeded him; Eden's government had lost the confidence of the United States.
Israel withdrew from Sinai and Gaza in early 1957, after the United States gave assurances about the Straits of Tiran and the UNEF presence.
The canal was blocked by sunken ships during the fighting and was cleared and reopened in 1957, under Egyptian control.
Nasser's prestige in the Arab world increased sharply because he had defied Britain, France and Israel and kept control of the canal.
Britain and France lost their position as the main Western powers in the Middle East, and the United States took a larger role there.
The crisis showed the limits of Anglo-French power after 1945, and it weakened the Anglo-French alliance with each other.

notes.b: Ben-Gurion led the Jewish community in Palestine and was the first prime minister of Israel.
points: Born David Grün in 1886 in Płońsk in the Russian Empire, he emigrated to Ottoman Palestine in 1906 and worked as a labour activist.
He led the Jewish Agency's executive from 1935 and accepted the partition plan of 1947 as a first step towards a Jewish state.
As a participant he proclaimed Israel on 14 May 1948, and he served as prime minister in 1948–53 and again in 1955–63; he also led the defence ministry.
He oversaw the Haganah's transformation into the Israel Defence Forces and planned the Israeli role in the Sinai campaign of 1956 with Britain and France.
Contemporary Arab opinion regarded him as the architect of a state that had displaced Palestinians, while many Jews in Palestine and in the diaspora saw him as the founder of the state.

Historians debate his role in the flight of Palestinian Arabs in 1948, and they examine his statements about population transfer; his role in the Suez campaign is also judged critically as well as praised.

notes.b: Nasser was the leader of Egypt from 1954 to 1970 and the most important figure of Arab nationalism in the Suez crisis.
points: Born 15 January 1918 in Alexandria, he trained as an army officer and was one of the Free Officers who overthrew King Farouk in 1952.
As prime minister from 1954 and president from 1956, he pursued land reform, industrialisation and the building of the Aswan High Dam.
He was a participant in the Suez Crisis and in the Egyptian politics of the 1950s; he nationalised the canal and defied the Anglo-French invasion.
He formed the United Arab Republic with Syria in 1958, which lasted until 1961, and he supported anti-colonial movements in Algeria and elsewhere.
British ministers, including Eden, compared him with dictators of the 1930s, while Arab nationalists across the region saw him as a hero who had defied the West.
Historians differ on his legacy: some stress his social reforms and his anti-colonial stance, while others stress his authoritarian rule and the defeat of 1967.

notes.h: Assessment: British policy in Palestine and Suez
points: Achievement: Britain brought the Palestine Mandate to an end and passed the question to the UN, instead of prolonging an unworkable administration.
Limit: the Mandate's conflicting promises to Arabs and Jews were not reconciled, and the 1948 war left a legacy of refugees and hostility.
Achievement: the Anglo-French forces achieved their military objectives in Egypt within a week, and Israel's Sinai campaign was successful.
Limit: the Suez operation failed politically; the ceasefire was forced by the United States, the Soviet threat and the UN, and the canal remained in Egyptian hands.
Contemporary view: many in Britain believed that the government had acted to protect strategic interests; critics at home and abroad condemned the secret collusion with Israel.
Later view: historians generally see Suez as the point at which Britain's role as a world power was shown to be limited, although they debate how far Britain was responsible for Middle East tensions.

keyTerms.definition: The movement that sought a Jewish national homeland, which in the 1917–48 period centred on Palestine.
The use of violence against civilians or political targets to create fear and advance a political aim, used in Palestine by Jewish and Arab armed groups.
The British statement of 2 November 1917 supporting a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine.
The League of Nations system under which Britain administered Palestine from 1923 until 14 May 1948.
The movement for the political unity and independence of Arab peoples, which opposed both Western control and the state of Israel.
The transfer of a privately owned company or asset to state ownership, as in Nasser's takeover of the Suez Canal Company in 1956.
The secret agreement of October 1956 among Britain, France and Israel that set out the military plan for the invasion of Egypt.
The United Nations Emergency Force, set up in November 1956 to supervise the withdrawal of the invading forces and the Sinai frontier.
